Once the site was deemed safe, the path was laid for construction on the first of the terminals, runways, and a control tower. There's no denying the terminals are going to be visually remarkable, but they definitely don't come cheap. Concrete becomes very brittle when you put it into a curved situation. And as you can imagine with something like steel, the thicker it is, the harder it is to manipulate because of its increased density. The nation was nearing the beginning of its journey to economic growth. Trade was increasing and poverty was in decline. But residents worried the long-term debts loaded onto the government through loans for long term could set the nation back. And while Vietnam is continuing its financial evolution, there are still concerns over the massive price tag attached to this airport. video_upload_date: The $2BN Airport Built in a Swamp
column8: Did India build Navi Mumbai International in the worst place possible?🔥 Pre-order Fred's book MEGA BUILDS now 👉 https://bit.ly/3Y63G6XFull story here - htt...
column10: This might just be India's answer to Changi. It's called Navim Mumbai International Airport and it opened its terminals to passengers in December last year. The place looks pretty stunning and that's just phase 1. Once the final phase is complete, Navi Mumbai will welcome an astounding 90 million passengers a year, 20 million more than Changi. India wants this to become a hub for world travel. Now, you'd be right to raise an eyebrow to any newcomer being compared to Singapore's Pride and Joy. That is arguably the best airport in the world. But don't forget that Changi was a military air base long before it became a civilian facility. The engineers behind Navi Mumbai could only dream of building on an air base. Their reality was entirely different. They were tasked with building an airport on a swamp covered in unstable mud flats, a giant hill, and a river flowing right through the middle of it. While the renders of Navi Mumbai International look spectacular, this airport's location has been an absolute nightmare. India has one of the fastest growing aviation sectors on the planet behind only China and the US. The number of operational airports in the country has doubled in the last decade as Prime Minister Narendra Modi looks set to overhaul India's travel infrastructure. Mumbai, its financial powerhouse is under resourced. A number of the world's most prominent cities feature multiple major airports. Think London, New York or Tokyo. And that's obviously crucial for visitor numbers, business trips and cargo. Let's take London for example. The city is serviced by six major airports. All of those combined handled a whopping 177 million passengers in 2024. Mumbai, however, has historically had just one major airport. That would be like London having just Heathrow. The city would miss out on nearly 100 million passengers every year. And given that rapidly growing aviation sector in India, the country is desperate to improve capacity to its financial capital. The answer authorities came up with was simple. a second major airport in Mumbai. But executing an idea of this scale is rarely as straightforward as having the epiphany itself. The biggest problem faced by Mumbai's second big airport plan is experienced by major cities all around the world. The lack of space. Just take a look at Mumbai airport which is already at capacity. Terminal one over here is going through a redevelopment, but there isn't exactly a lot of scope for expanding the footprints. On every side, there are densely packed communities that would be a nightmare to move, and it's not like they didn't try. That evidence can be found over at Terminal 2. The concourses here are asymmetrical. The initial plan was for them to be the same length, but because of the challenges faced in moving communities on the airport boundary, the second concourse had to be redesigned. It looks like it's been cut off and that obviously limits the number of gates that are available. Air traffic is also pretty restricted because of the intersecting runways. The design stops planes landing and taking off on each strip at the same time. And as we pointed out, it's not like there's a lot of space to build parallel runways elsewhere. The result is that Mumbai is missing out on potentially millions of passengers and tons of cargo every year, and the city's key airport really is crying out for help. But clearly a major expansion is out of the question, as is constructing a massive new airport anywhere near the city center. So where do you go? Well, after a 10year search and then a further 3 years spent buying up land, officials ended up here. It's about 40 km away from the old commercial center of Mumbai over in Nav'i Mumbai. In what's become a growing trend over the last decade, the Nav'i Mumbai international site is on the coast. That means it's built largely on reclaimed land and that's required a lot of preparation. Now, before we go any further with today's video, we need to stop everything because I have got some very big news that I am finally allowed to share. Last year, Penguin Random House asked me if I'd like to write a book. I said yes. I've written a book and here it is. It is called Mega Builds: 10 Colossal Construction Projects That Will Change World. Over the last 10 years, I have had a front row seat to some of this planet's most incredible construction projects, and they are all in here. I've written about them. I've gone deeper than I've ever gone before in any video story or any kind of like long- form documentary. This is behind the scenes. It's up close and personal. It meets the teams. It's the human stories. It's the engineering in detail. It's my personal experiences and some of the calamities I've had along the way getting up close with these projects. I have really enjoyed writing this. Some of my mates have been like, "Oh, nice. Who uh who ghost wrote that for you?" No one. I can't afford a fancy ghost writer. Me. I wrote this. Every single word of this has come from my head into my laptop and then into this book. All for your reading pleasure. Guys, I never thought I could write a book, but I have. And obviously, I'm biased, but I actually kind of think it's quite good. It is available to pre-order now. The link is below. Pre-ordering is incredibly important. Basically, my entire future happiness depends on you pre-ordering this book. So guys, if you love the B1M, if you love these stories, if you love learning more about construction in a downto-earth way that's easy to understand and can be read by anyone, go and pre-order my book, Mega Builds, today. Before any work could start on the foundations back in 2018, three key hurdles had to be tackled, and each of them was pretty massive. We Hill, Swampland, and Ol River. Let's start here. Right in the middle of the site for the new airport, you'd find this all hill. It's 92 m of solid rock. Obviously, having a hill in the middle of your concourse isn't exactly ideal. So, that had to be completely flattened before any building could take place. Construction crews demolished 62 million cub m of rock through controlled blasting to protect surrounding villages. But once that was finished, the site looks like this. So, on to problem number two. What do you do with the blasted rock? Well, it was repurposed. You see, hundreds of acres of this airport sit on swamp land. It's covered in mud flats and mangroves, all of which have got to be leveled and stabilized before construction work can begin. To do that, they had to raise the ground by around 6 m. And conveniently, they had enormous amounts of rock available from that big old hill they' just blown up. What's really cool is that these guys blasted the rock at specific explosive power designations to create rock fragments that were the ideal size for land development and reclamation. The blasted rock was basically dumped into marshy areas, puncturing and displacing the soft clay. The weight of all that rock then compacted the soil, making it stronger and reducing the amount of intensive treatment that was needed to thicken any weak ground. But that wasn't the final hurdle. This is River in 2019. Originally, it cut through the middle of the site, but beyond acting as an interesting water feature, a river through a runway is actually incredibly impractical. Engineers were left with no choice but to redirect it. You can see it's been cut at an angle, diverting around the site. And if you're thinking it now looks bigger, then you'd be right. Navim Mumbai Airport is surrounded by villages whose people have watched this site completely transform. But within those communities, there's a very real concern about flooding. It's effective to produce at scale, but slightly translucent and at best only reflects around 40% [music] of light. In other words, it'll never be as good as this. This is Mariah. Plus, it'll only have two stations, meaning it's not much use for people that live in the middle of the city. It means that for those other services, you're stuck using a suburban train that stops every 1.5 km or roughly every mile. How efficient is that? So, where are we? column10: I'm currently standing in a massive tunnel deep beneath the Alps. When it's finished, this incredible feat of construction is going to stretch for more than 50 km and bring two major European countries close together. It's because the tunnel forms the main section of a new railway [music] that will literally cut journey times between these two places in half. In a few years from now, it'll become the longest single rail tunnel [music] in the world. But how exactly you build a train line through a mountain range? [music] I've come to one of the world's biggest construction projects to see how teams are pulling it off. We're digging through the middle of a mountain [music] and to discover the incredible impact it's going to have not just for the countries either side, but for this wider continent, too. Wa! Look at this. [music] This is quite literally my deepest dive yet into one of this planet's biggest mega belts. >> [music] >> So, I'm currently on a little road trip between France and Italy. I'm driving from Leyon, which is back there behind me. You can see it here on the map. And I'm going to be going along this road all the way here to Trin in Italy. Now, that road is the quickest and easiest way currently to get between these two places, but it's not straightforward because what you can't see on this map is that sitting between these two cities are the mighty Alps. Now, don't get me wrong, it is a beautiful drive, but it takes you about 4 hours, and it would be the same if you were to go by train. However, it's not going to stay that for much longer because construction teams are now working on a new railway underneath this natural border, and they're doing it with a record-breaking tunnel. France and Italy are two of the largest economies on the planet, and they're situated right next to each other. But despite that, and the fact they're both part of the EU, moving people and goods between them isn't exactly straightforward. And it's because of those mountains. It's a difficult place to build a road, let alone a railway, which is why 92% of all freight movement between Italy and France is done by truck. Now, I probably don't need to tell you that road transportation is both worse for the environment and slower than going by train. So, something is finally being done about it, but it means going to some pretty extreme lengths. Now, as I said earlier, there already is a way to get from Lyon to Trin by train, as long as you don't mind traveling on a line that was built in the 1800s and is nowhere near highspeed because it's full of winding curves and steep slopes. Not to mention the landslides, which are a very real threat here. The one that happened in 2023 was so severe it caused the whole railway to shut down for a year and a half. Now, obviously, the way we build our railways has changed massively since the 19th century. Trains today are not just faster, safer, and more comfortable, but they can get across difficult terrain that just wouldn't have been possible all those years ago. Now, a lot of it is down to new tunneling techniques. But here in the Alps, engineers have been perfecting an approach that takes underground construction to a whole new level. They're called base tunnels, which comes from the fact that they burrow right through the base of a mountain. It means the tracks can be laid almost flat and that enables faster trains and short journeys. And that's exactly what's been under construction here. Halfway between Leon and Serin across the French Italian border. Stretching for 57.5 km, it'll become the longest single rail tunnel in [music] the world. A fraction longer than the Gotard base tunnel in Switzerland. Although that one is almost a decade old, it remains one of the only base tunnels to have been completed on this planet.
